implementation_notes: database/sql gives the boundary and nothing else: DB.BeginTx returns an sql.Tx whose Exec and Query run on one connection until Commit or Rollback, and the Go documentation tells you to defer tx.Rollback, never to issue BEGIN/COMMIT through raw SQL, and never to mix non-transaction DB calls into the same work. There is no identity map and no dirty checking, so the register half is a struct you write: a map keyed by primary key holding new, dirty and removed rows plus a Commit method that walks the lists in foreign-key order. GORM adds closure and Begin/Commit helpers and wraps each write in its own transaction by default, which is convenient but not a deferred flush - it saves eagerly, so batching still requires an explicit Transaction or Session around the calls.
pitfalls: One stray db.Exec (or a pool query) inside the unit of work commits immediately outside the Tx and breaks atomicity - pass the *sql.Tx everywhere.
defer tx.Rollback() after a successful Commit returns sql.ErrTxDone, which must be ignored rather than treated as a failure.
sql.Tx is not safe for concurrent use by multiple goroutines: one unit of work per request/goroutine.
GORM's default per-write transaction gives no batching benefit; use Transaction/Session deliberately, or disable it globally when the unit of work owns the boundary.

variants.name: GORM Transaction closure / Begin-Commit with explicit saves
variants.implementation_notes: GORM's Transaction closure commits when the callback returns nil and rolls back on any error, and nested Transaction calls use savepoints (SavePoint/RollbackTo are available manually). Model writes are still eager - tx.Create/tx.Save issue SQL immediately - so the unit of work is the closure plus your own tracking of what to save, not a deferred flush. Prefer it when GORM is already the persistence layer and the transaction is one service call.
pitfalls: Inside the callback you must use tx, never db, or the statement escapes the transaction and commits on its own.
GORM wraps every individual write in its own transaction unless SkipDefaultTransaction is set, so a sequence of writes without an outer Transaction is not atomic.
